LFP Compression: Functional Validation via Neural Decoding

electrophysiology
LFP
compression
Neuropixels
decoding
Does lossy LFP compression degrade downstream decoding of behaviour? Wheel speed, choice and feedback decoded from band-power envelopes across 11 benchmark recordings, uncompressed vs default vs aggressive SVD+WP compression.
Author

Olivier Winter

Published

August 31, 2026

Overview

The SVD/WP compression benchmark calibrates ε/α against RMSE and SNR — a spatial/amplitude fidelity proxy. That proxy says nothing about whether the information downstream analyses actually use survives compression. This page checks that directly: for each of the same 11 benchmark PIDs, wheel speed, choice and feedback are decoded from LFP band-power envelopes under three variants of the same recording —

  • uncompressed — lf_resampled_car_cadzow.npy (250 Hz, CAR + Cadzow-denoised, no lossy step)
  • default — ε=150, α=28 (CR ≈ 80–130×), the shipped BWM release default pass
  • aggressive — ε=450, α=96 (CR ≈ 200–430×), the shipped BWM release aggressive pass

Bottom line: the default pass tracks the uncompressed baseline closely on every target; the aggressive pass measurably erodes decoding, most severely for feedback. RMSE/CR alone would not have surfaced this — see Interpretation.

Method

Features. Same pipeline as the pynapple LFP decoding walkthrough (ibldevtools/olivier/2026-08-28_LFP_decoding_pynapple.py): LFP is spatially binned 384→96 channels (sum of 4 adjacent electrodes, matching lfpack’s bin_channels=4), then band-pass filtered (4th-order Butterworth) and Hilbert-enveloped in four bands (delta 1–4 Hz, theta 4–8 Hz, beta 15–30 Hz, gamma 30–90 Hz), log-transformed, and stacked into a 384-dim feature vector (96 channels × 4 bands) per timepoint. Saturated spans are excluded via LFPackReader.saturation_times().

Sample times for the uncompressed/default/aggressive variants (which predate lfpack’s sync-metadata write, so t0 is nan) are reconstructed from the raw probe clock via SpikeSortingLoader.timesprobe2times, using that decimated sample j corresponds to raw LF sample j × Q (Q=10) at 2500 Hz.

Targets and decoders.

Target Feature window Decoder CV Metric
|wheel velocity| continuous, 50 ms bins RidgeCV (α ∈ logspace(-2,4,20)) 5-fold chronological R²
choice [-0.2, 0) s rel. firstMovement_times, nogo excluded Standardized LogisticRegressionCV 5-fold stratified balanced accuracy
feedback [0, 0.2) s rel. feedback_times Standardized LogisticRegressionCV 5-fold stratified balanced accuracy

Null. A simple per-fold label/target shuffle (20 shuffles for the categorical targets). This is not a pseudo-session control — it doesn’t preserve trial-to-trial autocorrelation, so it under-states significance for any single recording. That’s an acceptable trade-off here: the question is the relative effect of compression on the same decode, not whether any one recording’s decode is itself significant, and the null is held identical across all three variants of a given recording/target.

Feedback decoding degrades monotonically and substantially: median balanced accuracy 0.568 (uncompressed) → 0.542 (default) → 0.508 (aggressive) — the aggressive-tier distribution collapses almost entirely to chance. Choice shows the same direction but is weaker throughout (median 0.546 → 0.533 → 0.509) and several recordings are already near chance uncompressed, so there is less to lose. One recording (d7ec0892) decodes both targets strongly and stays well above chance even under aggressive compression (feedback 0.86 → 0.83 → 0.74), showing the effect is a graded erosion, not a hard floor.

Interpretation

Feedback — decoded from a brief post-event window — is the target most sensitive to compression; wheel speed — a slower, broadband state variable averaged over 50 ms bins — is the least. This lines up with the WP-stage mechanism described in index.qmd §Adaptive WP threshold calibration: the per-coefficient threshold τ_k = α·σ₀/s_k discards low-magnitude wavelet coefficients first, and fine time-scale (higher-frequency) structure is exactly where LFP wavelet coefficients tend to be smallest. Raising α from 28 (default) to 96 (aggressive) doesn’t just lower CR uniformly — it disproportionately removes the fast, phasic content that a post-event classifier like the feedback decoder depends on, while barely touching the slow band-power fluctuations wheel-speed decoding uses. RMSE, being dominated by the (larger-amplitude) slow components, is largely blind to this — it does not distinguish “lost 5 µV of slow drift” from “lost the phasic transient that carries the feedback signal.”

Conclusion

The default pass (ε=150, α=28) is functionally safe for the decoding uses checked here. The aggressive pass (ε=450, α=96) is not: it measurably degrades wheel-speed decoding and substantially degrades feedback decoding, without a corresponding warning from the RMSE/CR metric it was calibrated on. Recommendation: retire the current aggressive tier for any downstream use that touches decoding, and calibrate a new intermediate tier using a decoding-aware objective rather than RMSE alone — see Next steps.

Next steps

Proposed approach for calibrating an intermediate tier, not yet run:

  1. Change the objective. Sweep candidate (ε, α) pairs and score each by decoding loss relative to uncompressed (ΔR² for wheel speed, Δbalanced-accuracy for choice/feedback) at a given CR, rather than RMSE. Feedback balanced accuracy is the most sensitive of the three metrics found here, so it should anchor the acceptance criterion (e.g. no more than a fixed fraction of the uncompressed decode retained).
  2. Sweep α more finely than ε. §Interpretation points at α (the WP stage, which governs how much fine temporal/high-frequency structure survives within each retained SVD component) as the more likely lever for the feedback-decoding cost, not ε (which mainly sets spatial rank). A useful first pass: fix ε at its default 150 and sweep α between 28 and 96 (e.g. {28, 40, 55, 70, 96}), before touching ε at all.
  3. Keep the search cheap. The full decode (band envelopes + 3 decoders) costs ~10 min/recording/variant, so an 11-PID × full-α-grid sweep is expensive. Run the α sweep on 3–4 recordings chosen to span the observed decodability range (e.g. d7ec0892 — strong decoder throughout; 1e104bf4 or da8dfec1 — weak decoder, most likely to show a floor effect; one mid-range recording), then confirm the selected operating point on the full 11-PID benchmark used throughout this page.
  4. Report CR alongside decoding loss, not RMSE alongside decoding loss — RMSE has already been shown here to miss the effect that matters; keep it as a secondary sanity check rather than the selection criterion.

## Results

### Continuous target: wheel speed

```{python}
#| echo: false
import pandas as pd

wheel = pd.read_csv("2026-08-31_decoding_metrics_wheel.csv")
order = ["uncompressed", "default", "aggressive"]
wheel.pivot(index="pid", columns="variant", values="r2")[order].round(3)
```

Median R² drops only slightly from uncompressed (0.134) through default (0.133) to aggressive
(0.084) — the default pass is functionally indistinguishable from uncompressed for this
target, and even aggressive stays well above the shuffled null (always negative) in every
recording.

![Wheel-speed decoding R² per recording and compression tier, vs shuffled null (black ticks).](figures/2026-08-31_lfp-compression-decoding_r2-by-pid.png){.lightbox}

![R² distribution across the 11 recordings, one box per compression tier.](figures/2026-08-31_lfp-compression-decoding_r2-boxplot.png){.lightbox}

![Measured vs decoded \|wheel velocity\|, 60 s windows, three example recordings. Default and aggressive traces track the uncompressed decode closely; all three miss the sharpest movement peaks.](figures/2026-08-31_lfp-compression-decoding_wheel-overlay.png){.lightbox}

### Categorical targets: choice and feedback

```{python}
#| echo: false
cat = pd.read_csv("2026-08-31_decoding_metrics_categorical.csv")
cat.pivot_table(index="pid", columns=["target", "variant"], values="balanced_accuracy")[
    [(t, v) for t in ["choice", "feedback"] for v in order]
].round(3)
```

![Choice / feedback balanced accuracy across the 11 recordings, one box per compression tier. Dashed line = chance.](figures/2026-08-31_lfp-compression-decoding_categorical_boxplot.png){.lightbox}

Feedback decoding degrades monotonically and substantially: median balanced accuracy 0.568
(uncompressed) → 0.542 (default) → 0.508 (aggressive) — the aggressive-tier distribution
collapses almost entirely to chance. Choice shows the same direction but is weaker throughout
(median 0.546 → 0.533 → 0.509) and several recordings are already near chance uncompressed, so
there is less to lose. One recording (`d7ec0892`) decodes both targets strongly and stays well
above chance even under aggressive compression (feedback 0.86 → 0.83 → 0.74), showing the
effect is a graded erosion, not a hard floor.

## Interpretation {#interpretation}

Feedback — decoded from a brief post-event window — is the target most sensitive to
compression; wheel speed — a slower, broadband state variable averaged over 50 ms bins — is
the least. This lines up with the WP-stage mechanism described in
[index.qmd §Adaptive WP threshold calibration](index.qmd#adaptive-wp-threshold-calibration):
the per-coefficient threshold `τ_k = α·σ₀/s_k` discards low-magnitude wavelet coefficients
first, and fine time-scale (higher-frequency) structure is exactly where LFP wavelet
coefficients tend to be smallest. Raising α from 28 (default) to 96 (aggressive) doesn't just
lower CR uniformly — it disproportionately removes the fast, phasic content that a post-event
classifier like the feedback decoder depends on, while barely touching the slow band-power
fluctuations wheel-speed decoding uses. RMSE, being dominated by the (larger-amplitude) slow
components, is largely blind to this — it does not distinguish "lost 5 µV of slow drift" from
"lost the phasic transient that carries the feedback signal."

## Conclusion

The default pass (ε=150, α=28) is functionally safe for the decoding uses checked here. The
aggressive pass (ε=450, α=96) is not: it measurably degrades wheel-speed decoding and
substantially degrades feedback decoding, without a corresponding warning from the RMSE/CR
metric it was calibrated on. **Recommendation: retire the current aggressive tier** for any
downstream use that touches decoding, and calibrate a new intermediate tier using a
decoding-aware objective rather than RMSE alone — see
[Next steps](#next-steps).
